results.desc: hard link files instead of copying
results.question: How do I hard link files instead of copying using cp?

run.final:
# Hard Linking Files with `ln`

Use the `ln` command instead of `cp`:

```bash
ln source_file target_link
```

## Examples

```bash
# Create a hard link
ln /home/user/document.txt /home/user/document_link.txt

# Overwrite if target already exists
ln -f /home/user/document.txt /home/user/document_link.txt
```

## Key Differences from `cp`

| | `cp` (copy) | `ln` (hard link) |
|---|---|---|
| Inode | New inode | Same inode |
| Disk space | Duplicated | Shared |
| Cross-filesystem | ✅ Works | ❌ Fails |
| Directories | ✅ Works | ❌ Fails (on most systems) |
| Delete original | Link still valid | Link still valid (data persists) |

## Important Notes

- **Same filesystem required** — hard links cannot span different mounts/partitions.
- **Cannot link directories** (on Linux; some BSDs allow it with restrictions).
- **`ln -s`** creates a *symbolic* (soft) link instead, which *can* cross filesystems and link directories, but behaves differently (it's a pointer, not a second name for the same inode).

```bash
# Verify they share the same inode
ls -i /home/user/document.txt /home/user/document_link.txt
# 1234567 /home/user/document.txt
# 1234567 /home/user/document_link.txt
```

If you need cross-filesystem linking, use a symlink:

```bash
ln -s /home/user/document.txt /mnt/other_fs/document_link.txt
```

```
-L, --dereference
```

- **`-H`** (`--follow-symlink`): follow command-line symbolic links in SOURCE only
- **`-P`** (`--no-dereference`): never follow symbolic links in SOURCE (default behavior)

results.question: How do I stay on this file system using cp?

run.final:
Use the `--one-file-system` option:

```bash
cp --one-file-system -r /source /dest
```

This tells `cp` **not to cross file system boundaries** — it will skip any subdirectory that is a mount point for a different filesystem.

**Example:**

```bash
cp --one-file-system -r /home /backup
```

This copies `/home` but will **not** descend into, say, `/home/user/mnt` if that's a separate mount (e.g., a USB drive or network share).

**Common use case:** Backing up a directory tree while avoiding `/proc`, `/sys`, or other mounted filesystems:

```bash
cp --one-file-system -a / /backup
```

> **Note:** There is no short-form flag for this option in GNU `cp`. It's only available as `--one-file-system`.

## Showing the Enclosing C Function in a Diff

### With `git diff` (recommended)

`git diff` **already shows the enclosing function name** in the hunk header by default for C files:

```
@@ -10,7 +10,7 @@ int foo(int x)
```

If you want to show the **entire function body** as context (not just 3 lines), use:

```bash
git diff --function-context
```

or equivalently:

```bash
git diff --show-function-context
```

This makes the output look like:

```
@@ -10,20 +10,20 @@ int foo(int x)
 {
     int a = 1;
     int b = 2;
-    return a + b;
+    return a * b;
 }
```

### How it detects functions

Git uses a regex to find function definitions. For C, the default pattern is:

```
^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*\s*\([^)]*\)\s*$
```

You can customize it per-filetype with:

```bash
git config diff.c.fnreg '^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*\s*\([^)]*\)\s*$'
```

### With plain `diff` (GNU diffutils)

1. **Use `git diff`** on the two files:
   ```bash
   git diff --no-index old.c new.c
   ```

2. **Use `git diff` with `--function-context`**:
   ```bash
   git diff --no-index --function-context old.c new.c
   ```

| Function name in hunk header | `git diff` (default) |
| Full function as context | `git diff --function-context` |
| Non-git files | `git diff --no-index --function-context a.c b.c` |

run.final:
The option is **`-n`** (or `--no-name`).


**Why:** By default, gzip stores the original filename and modification timestamp in the file header. Using `-n` omits the filename and timestamp from the header, making the output **deterministic** — the same input always produces the same output, so rsync can correctly detect that nothing has changed.

Use the **`-l`** (or `--list`) option:

```bash
gzip -l *.gz

# List and keep original files (no-op for listing, but useful in scripts)
gzip -lk file.gz
```

The `-l` flag is read-only — it does **not** modify or decompress the file.

run.final:
# Running `wget` in the Background

## Quick & Simple

```bash
wget -O output.html http://example.com/file &
```

The `&` sends the process to the background immediately.

## Surviving Terminal Close (most common need)

```bash
nohup wget -O output.html http://example.com/file > wget.log 2>&1 &
```

- `nohup` — prevents the process from being killed when you close the terminal
- `> wget.log 2>&1` — redirects output (including errors) to a log file
- `&` — runs in background

## Using `disown`

```bash
wget -O output.html http://example.com/file &
disown
```

This detaches the job from the shell's job table so it won't be killed on logout.

## Using `screen` or `tmux` (for long downloads)

```bash
screen -S mydownload
wget -O output.html http://example.com/file
# Press Ctrl+A, then D to detach
```

Reattach later with `screen -r mydownload`.

## As a systemd service (for automated/recurring use)

Create `/etc/systemd/system/wget-download.service`:

```ini
[Unit]
Description=Download file with wget
After=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/bin/wget -O /path/to/output.html http://example.com/file
RemainAfterExit=yes

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

Then:
```bash
sudo systemctl enable --now wget-download
```

## Checking on it

```bash
# Find the process
ps aux | grep wget

# Or if you used nohup, check the log
tail -f wget.log
```

---

**TL;DR** — For most cases, just use:

```bash
nohup wget -O output.html http://example.com/file > wget.log 2>&1 &
```

## Use the `-0` (or `--null`) option

```bash

```

### What it does

From the GNU `xargs` man page:

> **`-0, --null`**
> Input items are terminated by a null character instead of by whitespace, and the quotes and backslash are not special (every character is taken literally). Disables the end-of-file string, which is treated like any other argument. Useful when input items might contain white space, quote marks, or backslashes. The GNU `find -print0` option produces input suitable for this mode.

So `-0` gives you exactly the three behaviors you described:

1. **Items are separated by a null byte (`\0`)**, not whitespace.
2. **Quote and backslash processing is disabled** — every character is taken literally.
3. **Logical EOF processing is disabled** — the end-of-file string (normally set with `-E`/`-e`) is treated like any other argument.

### Typical usage

Pair it with `find -print0`, which emits null-terminated paths:

```bash
find . -name '*.txt' -print0 | xargs -0 rm
```

This safely handles filenames containing spaces, newlines, quotes, or backslashes.

If you need a custom delimiter (not just null), use `-d`:

```bash

```

`-d` also disables quote/backslash processing and the end-of-file string, but it lets you pick any single character (or C-style escape like `\n`, or octal/hex codes) as the separator. The man page notes that `--null` is almost always the better choice when possible.

results.desc: test zipfile integrity
results.question: How do I test zipfile integrity using zip?

run.final:
## Testing Zipfile Integrity with `zip`

Use the **`-T`** flag:

```bash
zip -T archive.zip
```

This tests the integrity of `archive.zip` by verifying the CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check) of each file in the archive.

### Example

```bash
$ zip -T myarchive.zip
testing: myarchive.zip
  atime: 2024-01-15:10:30:00
  ctime: 2024-01-15:10:30:00
  mtime: 2024-01-15:10:30:00
  size: 12345
  crc: 0xabcdef12
  ok
```

### Useful combinations

| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `zip -T archive.zip` | Test integrity (default) |
| `zip -T -v archive.zip` | Verbose output (shows each file tested) |
| `zip -T -q archive.zip` | Quiet mode (only shows errors) |

### Exit codes

- **0** — All files passed the integrity check
- **Non-zero** — One or more files failed (corrupted)

### Note

`zip -T` checks the **CRC-32** checksums stored in the archive. It does **not** verify the actual file contents against the original source files — it only confirms that the compressed data in the archive is internally consistent (i.e., not corrupted).

results.question: What is the difference between a process and a thread?

run.final:
# Process vs. Thread

## Process

A **process** is an instance of a program in execution. It is the fundamental unit of resource allocation in an operating system.

- Has its own **virtual address space** (memory is isolated from other processes)
- Has its own file descriptors, environment variables, and other resources
- Communication between processes requires **IPC** (pipes, shared memory, sockets, etc.)
- Heavier to create and destroy
- A crash in one process typically does **not** affect others

## Thread

A **thread** (or lightweight process) is a unit of execution *within* a process.

- Shares the **same address space** as other threads in the same process
- Shares file descriptors, global variables, and heap
- Communication is trivial (just read/write shared memory)
- Lighter to create and destroy
- A crash in one thread (e.g., segfault) **can** crash the entire process

## Key Differences at a Glance

| Aspect | Process | Thread |
|---|---|---|
| Memory | Isolated | Shared |
| Creation cost | Higher | Lower |
| Communication | IPC required | Direct (shared memory) |
| Isolation | Strong | Weak |
| Scheduling | OS schedules processes | OS schedules threads (or user-space scheduler) |
| Context switch | More expensive (TLB flush, etc.) | Cheaper (shared page tables) |

## Analogy

Think of a **process** as a company with its own office building (memory, resources). A **thread** is an employee within that company — they share the same building, tools, and files, but each can work on a different task simultaneously.

## Why It Matters

- **Concurrency**: Threads let you parallelize work within a single program without the overhead of inter-process communication.
- **Safety**: Processes give you isolation — a bug in one doesn't take down the others (this is why browsers use a process-per-tab model).
- **Performance**: Threads avoid the cost of copying data between address spaces, but you must handle synchronization (mutexes, atomics) to avoid data races.

run.final: A race condition is a bug in concurrent or parallel programming where the correctness of a program depends on the relative timing or interleaving of events that are not guaranteed to occur in a particular order. For example, if two threads simultaneously read a shared variable, both modify it, and write it back, the final value may depend on which thread's write happens last — and if the program's logic assumes a specific outcome, the result is unpredictable. The term "race" comes from the idea that the threads are "racing" to access or modify shared state, and the one that "wins" determines the outcome. Race conditions are notoriously difficult to debug because they are non-deterministic: the bug may appear only under specific timing conditions, making it seem to work fine in testing while failing intermittently in production. Common mitigations include using locks, atomic operations, or designing systems to avoid shared mutable state altogether.

run.final:
## Idempotent HTTP Methods

**Idempotent** means that making the same request multiple times produces the **same result** as making it once. The server's state after *N* identical requests is the same as after *1* request.

### Idempotent methods

| Method | Why it's idempotent |
|--------|-------------------|
| `GET` | Reading a resource doesn't change state |
| `PUT` | Replacing a resource with the same body yields the same result |
| `DELETE` | Deleting an already-deleted resource is a no-op |
| `HEAD` | Same as GET but without the body |
| `OPTIONS` | Just returns metadata |

### Non-idempotent methods

| Method | Why it's not idempotent |
|--------|------------------------|
| `POST` | Each call typically creates a **new** resource |
| `PATCH` | Depends on the operation (e.g., "increment by 1" is not idempotent) |

### Practical example

```
PUT /users/42  {"name": "Alice"}   →  200 OK
PUT /users/42  {"name": "Alice"}   →  200 OK   (same result, no duplication)

POST /users     {"name": "Alice"}   →  201 Created  /users/43
POST /users     {"name": "Alice"}   →  201 Created  /users/44  (new resource each time)
```

### Why it matters

- **Retries are safe.** If a client times out and retries a `PUT` or `DELETE`, it won't cause duplicate side effects.
- **Caching.** Idempotent methods can be safely cached.
- **Design guidance.** If you need a "create" operation that's safe to retry, use `PUT` with a client-generated ID instead of `POST`.

### Key distinction

> Idempotent ≠ Idempotent in the mathematical sense of "f(f(x)) = f(x)" for all x.
> In HTTP, it means: **repeating the same request (same method, same URI, same body) has the same effect as a single request.**

This is defined in [RFC 9110 §9.2.2](https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html#idempotent).

results.question: Why is binary search O(log n)?

run.final:
## Why Binary Search is O(log n)

The core reason: **each comparison eliminates half of the remaining search space.**

### Step-by-step intuition

Suppose you're searching in a sorted array of `n` elements:

| Step | Elements remaining |
|------|-------------------|
| Start | n |
| After 1 comparison | n/2 |
| After 2 comparisons | n/4 |
| After 3 comparisons | n/8 |
| ... | ... |
| After k comparisons | n / 2ᵏ |

You stop when only 1 element remains:

```
n / 2ᵏ = 1
2ᵏ = n
k = log₂(n)
```

So the number of comparisons needed is **log₂(n)**.

### Concrete example

For n = 1,000,000:

- Linear search: up to 1,000,000 comparisons
- Binary search: log₂(1,000,000) ≈ **20 comparisons**

Each step "halves" the problem, so the number of steps grows logarithmically with the input size.

### The recurrence relation

Formally, the time satisfies:

```
T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)
```

- `T(n/2)` — the recursive call on half the array
- `O(1)` — the single comparison at each step

By the Master Theorem (or simple unrolling), this solves to **T(n) = O(log n)**.

### The key requirement

This only works because the array is **sorted**. That's what lets you decide "go left" or "go right" with a single comparison, discarding half the elements. Without sorting, you can't safely eliminate half the space, and you're back to O(n).

# TCP vs UDP

## TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)

- **Connection-oriented**: Establishes a connection (three-way handshake: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK) before data transfer.
- **Reliable**: Guarantees delivery via acknowledgments, retransmissions, and sequence numbers.
- **Ordered**: Data is delivered in the order it was sent.
- **Flow control**: Uses sliding window to prevent overwhelming the receiver.

# Printing File Names with `grep`

## Basic: Force filename display

Use the `-H` (or `--with-filename`) flag:

```bash
grep -H "pattern" file.txt
```

Output:
```
file.txt:matching line here
```

> **Note:** When you pass **multiple files**, `grep` shows filenames by default. `-H` is mainly useful when searching a **single file** and you still want the name shown.

## Common combinations

| Goal | Command |
|------|---------|
| Filename + line number | `grep -Hn "pattern" file.txt` |
| Recursive search (shows filenames automatically) | `grep -r "pattern" directory/` |
| Only list filenames that have matches | `grep -l "pattern" *.txt` |
| Recursive + only filenames | `grep -rl "pattern" directory/` |

## Examples

```bash
# Search a single file, show filename
grep -H "error" app.log
# → app.log:2024-01-01 ERROR: something failed

# Search multiple files (filenames shown automatically)
grep "error" *.log
# → app1.log:ERROR: timeout
# → app2.log:ERROR: null pointer

# Recursive search in a directory
grep -rn "TODO" src/
# → src/main.c:42: TODO: refactor this
# → src/utils.c:10: TODO: add error handling
```

## Quick reference

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `-H` | Always show filename |
| `-h` | Never show filename (suppress it) |
| `-l` | Show only filenames (no matching lines) |
| `-n` | Show line numbers |
| `-r` | Search recursively |

run.final:
Use the `--list-fields` option:

```bash
journalctl --list-fields
```

This prints a list of all field names (keys) currently present in the journal, one per line, e.g.:

```
_AUDIT_LOGINUID
_AUDIT_SESSION
_BOOT_ID
_CMDLINE
_COMM
...
```

### Useful variations

- **Limit to a specific time range or unit** (the field list reflects only the matching entries):
  ```bash
  journalctl --list-fields --since "1 hour ago"
  journalctl --list-fields -u sshd
  ```

- **Show field names with their value counts** (requires a newer systemd; not always available):
  ```bash
  journalctl --list-fields --output=cat
  ```

- **Combine with a specific field to see its distinct values** (the companion to `--list-fields`):
  ```bash
  journalctl --list-catalog
  journalctl _SYSTEMD_UNIT=sshd.service
  ```

### Notes
- `--list-fields` only reports fields that exist in the journal entries you're querying, so adding filters like `-u`, `--since`, or `--unit` narrows the result.
- It reads the journal like any other query, so it respects the same access rules (e.g., you may need `sudo` to see all fields from system journals).

The companion option `--list-objects` (newer systemd) lists object names, and `--list-boots` lists boot IDs, if you need similar "list what's there" functionality.

run.final:
# Excluding Backup and Lock Files with `tar`

Use the `--exclude` option (or `-X` for a file list) to skip files matching patterns.

## Common Patterns

```bash
# Exclude common backup and lock file patterns
tar czf archive.tar.gz \
  --exclude='*.bak' \
  --exclude='*.swp' \
  --exclude='*.swo' \
  --exclude='*~' \
  --exclude='*.lock' \
  --exclude='*.orig' \
  --exclude='*.old' \
  --exclude='*.tmp' \
  --exclude='*.rej' \
  /path/to/directory
```

## Using a Pattern File (for many patterns)

```bash
# Create a file with one pattern per line
cat > /tmp/exclude.txt <<EOF
*.bak
*.swp
*.swo
*~
*.lock
*.orig
*.old
*.tmp
*.rej
*.o
*.so
*.pyc
__pycache__
EOF

tar czf archive.tar.gz --exclude-from=/tmp/exclude.txt /path/to/directory
```

## Key Options

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `--exclude=PATTERN` | Exclude files matching the glob pattern |
| `--exclude-from=FILE` | Read patterns from a file (one per line) |
| `--no-exclude` | Disable any default excludes |
| `--no-exclude-vcs` | Don't auto-exclude VCS dirs (`.git`, etc.) |

## Important Notes

- **Patterns are glob-based**, not regex. Use `*` for wildcards.
- **Order matters**: `--exclude` must come **before** the directory argument in some tar versions.
- **Case sensitivity**: Patterns are case-sensitive by default. Use `--no-wildcards` or add both cases if needed.
- **GNU tar** also supports `--exclude-vcs` (excludes `.git`, `.svn`, etc.) and `--exclude-vcs-ignores` (respects `.gitignore`).

## Quick Example

```bash
# Archive a project, excluding backups, locks, and VCS
tar czf project.tar.gz \
  --exclude='*.bak' \
  --exclude='*.swp' \
  --exclude='*~' \
  --exclude='*.lock' \
  --exclude='.git' \
  --exclude='__pycache__' \
  ./myproject
```

run.final:
**`wget` does not have a `--render-js` flag.** That option doesn't exist in any version of GNU Wget.

Wget is a simple HTTP/FTP client that downloads raw content — it does **not** execute JavaScript or render pages.

## What to use instead

If you need to download a page that requires JavaScript to render (e.g., content loaded dynamically via JS), you need a headless browser or a JS-capable tool:

### 1. **`curl` + a headless browser** (most common)
```bash
# Using headless Chrome/Chromium
chromium --headless --dump-dom "https://example.com" > output.html
```

### 2. **`wget` with a rendering proxy**
Some services (like [r.jina.ai](https://r.jina.ai)) render JS and return plain HTML:
```bash
wget -O output.html "https://r.jina.ai/https://example.com"
```

### 3. **`playwright` or `puppeteer`** (for scripting)
```python
# Python + Playwright
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch()
    page = browser.new_page()
    page.goto("https://example.com")
    page.wait_for_load_state("networkidle")
    content = page.content()
    browser.close()

with open("output.html", "w") as f:
    f.write(content)
```

### 4. **`wget` for static content only**
If the page is mostly static and JS only enhances it, plain `wget` may be sufficient:
```bash
wget -O output.html "https://example.com"
```

| Tool | Executes JS? |
|------|-------------|

run.final:
## `cp --parents`

The `--parents` flag copies a file **along with its full directory path** into the destination directory.

### Syntax

```bash
cp --parents SOURCE DESTINATION_DIR
```

### Example

```bash
# Without --parents:
cp /home/user/docs/report.txt /tmp/
# Result: /tmp/report.txt

# With --parents:
cp --parents /home/user/docs/report.txt /tmp/
# Result: /tmp/home/user/docs/report.txt
```

- It **recreates the full source path** under the destination directory.
- It works with multiple sources:
  ```bash
  cp --parents /etc/hosts /etc/resolv.conf /tmp/
  ```

- It's useful when you want to preserve the directory structure of the source files relative to the destination.
- It's commonly used in combination with `-a` (archive) to preserve attributes:
  ```bash

  ```

`--parents` is a **GNU coreutils** extension (not POSIX), so it's available on Linux and most Unix-like systems but **not** on macOS/BSD by default.

The `--no-pad` flag (short form `-N`) in `file` **disables the default column padding** that aligns the file type description at a fixed column.

## Default behavior (with padding)

By default, `file` pads the filename with spaces so that all descriptions start at the same column:

```
$ file /etc/passwd /etc/hosts
/etc/passwd: ASCII text
/etc/hosts:  ASCII text
```

Notice the extra space after `/etc/hosts:` to align the descriptions.

## With `--no-pad`

```
$ file --no-pad /etc/passwd /etc/hosts
/etc/passwd: ASCII text
/etc/hosts: ASCII text
```

The description starts immediately after the `: ` separator with no extra padding.

## When to use it

- **Scripting / parsing** — when you want predictable, minimal output (e.g., piping to `cut`, `awk`, or splitting on `: `).
- **Combining with `-b`** — if you're already using `--brief` (no filenames), padding is irrelevant, but `--no-pad` is harmless.
- **Combining with `-F`** — if you use a custom separator like `-F ' | '`, `--no-pad` ensures no extra spaces are added after it.

## Example in a script

```bash
# Get just the file type, no padding, no filename
file -b --no-pad /etc/passwd
# → ASCII text
```

In short: `--no-pad` just removes the cosmetic alignment spaces so output is compact and easier to parse.

results.desc: attempt run command in precise intervals
results.question: How do I use the --precise flag in watch?

run.final:
## The `--precise` flag in `watch`

The `--precise` (or `-p`) flag tells `watch` to **attempt to run the command at precise intervals**, rather than waiting for the command to finish before starting the next interval timer.

### Default behavior (without `--precise`)

By default, `watch` starts the timer **after** the command finishes. So if your command takes 0.5 seconds and you set `--interval 1`, the actual cycle time is ~1.5 seconds (0.5s command + 1s wait).

### With `--precise`

With `--precise`, `watch` starts the timer **immediately** and tries to keep the total cycle time at exactly the interval. So with `--interval 1`, the command will be re-run every 1 second regardless of how long it takes (as long as it finishes within that interval).

### Example

```bash
# Without --precise: cycle = command_time + interval
watch -n 1 date

# With --precise: cycle ≈ interval (command runs at precise 1-second intervals)
watch -n 1 --precise date
```

### When to use it

- When you need **consistent timing** (e.g., monitoring something where drift matters).
- When your command is **fast** (finishes well within the interval).

### Caveat

## The `--precise` flag in `watch`

The `--precise` (or `-p`) flag tells `watch` to **attempt to run the command at precise intervals**, rather than waiting for the command to finish before starting the next interval timer.

### Default behavior (without `--precise`)

By default, `watch` starts the timer **after** the command finishes. So if your command takes 0.5 seconds and you set `--interval 1`, the actual cycle time is ~1.5 seconds (0.5s command + 1s wait).

### With `--precise`

With `--precise`, `watch` starts the timer **immediately** and tries to keep the total cycle time at exactly the interval. So with `--interval 1`, the command will be re-run every 1 second regardless of how long it takes (as long as it finishes within that interval).

### Example

```bash
# Without --precise: cycle = command_time + interval
watch -n 1 date

# With --precise: cycle ≈ interval (command runs at precise 1-second intervals)
watch -n 1 --precise date
```

### When to use it

- When you need **consistent timing** (e.g., monitoring something where drift matters).
- When your command is **fast** (finishes well within the interval).

### Caveat

If the command takes **longer** than the interval, `--precise` can't help — `watch` will wait for it to finish before starting the next run. It's described as an *attempt*, not a guarantee.
